identity_rationale: Sigmund Freud, identified by Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality and The Origin and Development of Psychoanalysis (Harry W. Chase translation of the 1909 Clark lectures). Existing curated person ID reused; no new authority ID or namesake merger.

screening.role: Selection context only, not substantive proof or automatic identity resolution.

sources.note: New rereading: title, translator’s note and complete chapter I, printed pp. 1–4. German original 1921 and James Strachey English translation 1922 kept distinct; note records author-requested relocation of passages into footnotes. Chapter IV was read in the earlier accepted source review, but not newly reread here; remaining chapters unread. Universal and clinical claims not independently verified.

sources.title: Peter Gay interview, The Psychoanalytically Informed Historian, Clio’s Psyche
sources.note: Complete question/answer defining psychohistory read: Gay prefers a historian oriented toward psychoanalysis and treats it as an auxiliary discipline, rejecting reductionism and insisting on the external world and evidence. Other interview answers not fully read. Direct requests denied but browser text accessible. Gay’s evaluative remarks about Freud as historian are his judgments, not atlas facts.

sources.title: Freud Museum London, Who Was Sigmund Freud?
sources.note: Museum biographical passage checked: born 6 May 1856, died 23 September 1939; named work list dates Three Essays to 1905. Other work-list dates not adopted without edition checks. No full biography or monograph reading.

sources.title: British Psychoanalytical Society, Sigmund Freud dies
sources.note: Institutional timeline states 24 September 1939, conflicting by one day with the Freud Museum’s 23 September. Death year 1939 is secure; this packet conservatively records year precision and does not silently resolve the disagreement.

dated_facts.support: Publication metadata only; complete work unread.

dated_facts.support: 1910 publication is distinct from lecture delivery in September 1909; prior complete-five-lecture reading retained without claiming a new rereading.

dated_facts.support: Original German date from consulted English witness; German text uncollated.

dated_facts.label: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (James Strachey English translation)
dated_facts.support: English translation date and translator explicit; distinct from 1921 original.

substantive_relations.relationship: Makes individual psychology relational by including others as models, helpers, opponents and objects.
substantive_relations.note: Own Group Psychology chapter I read in full. Freud questions a sharp individual/group divide and an irreducible primitive group instinct; the explanation is attributed theory, not validated clinical evidence.

substantive_relations.relationship: Peter Gay treats psychoanalysis as an auxiliary resource for history while requiring evidence about the external social world.
substantive_relations.note: Named substantive reader Gay’s own interview answer read. This qualified reception claim does not equate psychoanalysis with an exhaustive historical explanation or endorse every Freudian hypothesis.

limits: Selected theoretical contributions and dated texts, with original, revised, translated and posthumous forms distinguished. Source notes state actual reading extent; no complete monograph or comprehensive reception survey is claimed. Existing collective relationships and source/roster qualifications remain.
